active_narratives.title: Fed Rate Path: Hiked Sep 16, and the 2027 Dots Are the Hawkish Part
active_narratives.summary: THE DEBATE RESOLVED IN THE THESIS'S DIRECTION: the Fed HIKED 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on Sep 16, 2026, UNANIMOUS 12-0 (FOMC statement, federalreserve.gov, PRIMARY) — its first increase since Jul 2023, after holding at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 over three dissents FOR a hike. The hike itself was ~93% priced and was NOT the surprise. THE HAWKISH ELEMENT IS THE SEP: the median fed funds projection is 4.1% for BOTH 2026 and 2027, against June's 3.8% and 3.6% — a +50bp revision to the 2027 median. With the post-hike midpoint at 3.875%, that implies ONE more 25bp hike this year and NO CUTS PROJECTED IN 2027 AT ALL. Statement language: 'Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal.' Other medians revised hawkish vs June: GDP 2.3/2.4, unemployment 4.1, PCE 3.7, core PCE 3.4. The data that got the Fed here still holds: August payrolls +162k vs ~55k consensus with July revised -23k to +21k and unemployment 4.1% (BLS, Sep 4), and August CPI headline +0.4% m/m / 3.4% y/y with core +0.3% m/m (vs 0.2% consensus) / 2.4% y/y (BLS, Sep 11) — say 'hot core', not 'hot headline'. DO NOT QUOTE A FOLLOW-ON HIKE PROBABILITY: post-meeting figures are reported inconsistently across outlets (Oct 45% / Dec 30% on Sep 16 vs >75% Dec on Sep 14).
active_narratives.thesis: The narrative's founding call — the next move is a HIKE, not a cut — was correct and has now been delivered, so the forward question moves one step out: not whether the Fed hikes, but whether the SEP's 4.1% median for both 2026 and 2027 survives contact with the data. That equal-median path is the live claim, because it prices one more hike this year and removes 2027 cuts entirely, which is a materially more hawkish curve than markets carried into the meeting. Zero cut probability at any 2026 meeting is not just intact — it is now extended through 2027 by the Committee's own projections. Read: a duration headwind for capex-intensive mega-caps, a funding-cost headwind for the SG banks, and a repricing risk for any thesis that assumes cuts. Falsifiable both ways: a soft core-PCE run that pulls the 2027 median back down, or a second hike delivered in Oct/Dec that confirms it. active_narratives.title: Hyperscaler AI Capex Sustainability: ~$730B 2026 Guides vs ROI and Funding-Cost Risk
active_narratives.summary: Hyperscaler AI capex has outgrown the original $1.7T-by-2030 framing so decisively that its author retired it: Dell'Oro nearly DOUBLED its data-center capex forecast to >$3T by 2030 on Aug 18, 2026 (from $1.7T in January, newly counting the AI-specialized cloud segment). The Big Four alone guide to roughly $730B in 2026 (Alphabet $195-205B, Amazon ~$220B after raising from ~$200B on Jul 30, Microsoft $175B for CALENDAR 2026, restated from ~$190B on a useful-life reclass with spend unchanged, Meta $130-145B after narrowing from $125-145B on Jul 29 — a $5B floor raise, per the release verbatim) and analysts project ~$1T in 2027 (a circulating '$1.15T' is Morgan Stanley's figure INCLUDING SpaceX as a new hyperscaler — not like-for-like). Semiconductor supply chains benefit directly, but ROI-validation and financing-cost concerns have intensified as the numbers grew — a WSJ report (~Aug 18) put ~$3T of off-balance-sheet, mostly AI-related commitments across nine top tech firms.
active_narratives.thesis: AI infrastructure spending remains a strong tailwind for semis, memory, optics and power infrastructure, but multiple-compression risk emerges if capex growth decelerates or demand does not materialise. The Q2 2026 print season is now COMPLETE and it resolved in favour of continuation: all four reported by 30 July and none guided down — Alphabet RAISED to $195-205B on 22 July flagging a significant further increase in 2027, Meta narrowed to $130-145B (from $125-145B — a $5B floor raise) on 29 July, Microsoft restated calendar-2026 capex to $175B on a useful-life reclass (buildings 15-to-25 years, effective FY2027) with spend unchanged, and Amazon RAISED to ~$220B on 30 July. Read the Amazon raise as a different kind: it was attributed to HIGHER MEMORY COSTS — paying more for the same capacity, not buying more — so it is a weaker demand signal than a unit-driven raise and it transmits to memory vendors rather than along the whole chain, though Jassy said Amazon still will not have enough capacity for 2026 demand. The live constraint has shifted from willingness to spend toward the cost of funding it — the ~$12B El Paso datacenter bond (precisely: $12.55B of notes at a 7.5% coupon priced Jul 27 by the BlackRock-led JV holdco, BlackRock 80% / Meta 20%) and Amazon's $25B July issue (order book peaked ~$62B, final ~$41B, with an extra-yield concession — cooler than its March deal) are the anchors, and Alphabet's debut A$5.5B Kangaroo bond (Aug 19) priced its 20-year tranche near 7% — long-dated money for an AAA-class issuer now costs ~7% in AUD. Rates compound this: the Fed is tightening, not easing (hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on Sep 16, 12-0, with the SEP median at 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027 — no 2027 cuts; see fed_rate_pivot for the rate path), which is a duration headwind for capex-intensive mega-caps. Funding datapoint (Sep 10): Oracle held FY27 capex $90-95B but capped NET cash capex at $70B as customers prepay or bring their own hardware — the funding burden shifting to customers. No Big-4 guide change as of Sep 14 (Bloomberg's REPORTED Microsoft >38GW-by-2032 capacity plan carries no dollar figure). A first guide-down or 'digestion' framing from any major hyperscaler would be a cluster-wide thesis-break check, not a single-ticker event.

active_narratives.title: US-China Semiconductor Supply Chain Reshaping: Tariffs vs. Foundry Demand
active_narratives.summary: US-China technology restrictions continue to reshape semiconductor supply chains, but the direction is mixed rather than uniformly escalating. ASML's standing 2030 ambition is EUR 44-60B revenue set at its Nov 2024 Investor Day and never revised — though the FY26 guide midpoint (~EUR 44B) already touches its floor — and Intel's 18A is in volume production, with High-NA EUV dual-qualified on a subset of 18A layers in Oregon (High-NA-DEPENDENT high-volume manufacturing is a 2027/14A story, not a current fact). Onshoring economics support equipment and memory capex. China's materials levers are NOT all retaliation: the helium export prohibition (MOFCOM/GAC Announcement No. 29 of 2026, HS 2804290010; in force since Jul 10, open-ended, no licensing path) is GLOBAL in scope and driven by the Qatar supply shock — MOFCOM says on record it targets no country — while the genuine trade-war channel is the suspension cliffs: rare-earth/magnet measures lapse 2026-11-10 and Ga/Ge/antimony 2026-11-27, both snapping back by default; note the ban on dual-use exports to US MILITARY end users and the tungsten/indium/rare-earth measures of early 2025 were never suspended, so 'controls are paused' is too broad.
active_narratives.thesis: Structural supply-chain tailwinds from US-China decoupling support the onshoring complex — Intel 18A and 14A, ASML EUV, Micron's >$250B cumulative US plan through 2035 (raised from ~$200B on Jul 9, 2026) — while elevated cost of capital constrains the multiple paid for that demand. The policy picture is two-directional and the 'officials speaking vs agencies acting' rule now needs a SPLIT: on Moonshot specifically it still holds (no designation, no docket), but the distillation/model-export lane has formal instruments — OSTP's NSTM-4 directive on adversarial distillation (Apr 23, 2026) and a BIS is-informed letter requiring licences for certain frontier US model exports including API access (Jun 12, 2026) — while open-WEIGHT models remain uncontrolled. The Hong Kong emergency order lapsed Jul 14 and MOFCOM tariff-cut consultations (~$30B each way) continue. The durable read stands: weight enacted measures over statements — and the enacted list grew: Section 232 tariffs on unmanned aircraft systems (proclamation Aug 13, in force Sep 3; 100%/25% with allied caps, components 25% from Feb 9, 2027; China not named on its face) join polysilicon (15% + minimum prices from Dec 4) and the November materials cliffs, and a Section 232 semiconductor proclamation is ALREADY in force but NARROW — signed Jan 14, effective Jan 15, 2026: 25% ad valorem on 'certain advanced computing chips and certain derivative products' listed in an Annex, with US data-center, R&D, repair, startup, consumer, civil-industrial and public-sector uses exempt, and a clause allowing 'broader tariffs on semiconductors' at 'a significant' rate plus a tariff-offset program if negotiations failed — so the POLITICO-reported 'comprehensive semiconductor tariffs' (Aug 27) would be that PHASE-2 broadening, not a first instrument, and it still has NO Federal Register docket through the Sep 18 issue; the new China tariffs being held back until after the Sep 24 Xi-Trump summit (Inside US Trade via Taipei Times, Sep 19) are a SECTION 301 excess-capacity action (~7.5% recommended, possibly up to ~20%), not a Section 232 semiconductor measure — do not conflate the two and Moonshot is negotiating a 30% revenue share with US hyperscalers (Reuters Aug 26) under blacklist threats that remain threats. On H200 exports to China the binding constraint is Beijing, not Washington — BIS has granted licences to 10+ Chinese firms but Beijing's posture is selective and NVIDIA recognizes zero China H200 revenue, excluding it from guidance entirely.

active_narratives.title: ECB and Fed Both Tightening: Level Gap, Not Direction, Drives the Euro
active_narratives.summary: ECB held the deposit rate at 2.25% on Jul 23, 2026 after hiking 25bp on Jun 11 — its first hike since 2023 — and then HIKED all three rates 25bp at the Sep 10 projection meeting, UNANIMOUS — deposit 2.50%, MRO 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%, effective Sep 16 (ECB statement). The divergence has INVERTED: this is a tightening bias, not an easing cycle, and while the rate-LEVEL premium persists (Fed 3.75-4.00% after the Sep 16 hike vs ECB 2.50%), both banks now lean the same way — so the divergence is about LEVEL and CONVICTION, not direction: both have now delivered, the ECB on Sep 10 and the Fed on Sep 16 (12-0, SEP median 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027 — see fed_rate_pivot), so the conviction gap has closed. Post-FOMC the euro IS expressing the LEVEL gap: EUR/USD fell every session Sep 15-18 (ECB reference rate 1.1539 → 1.1537 → 1.1481 → 1.1460) with DXY 100.23 on Sep 18 (tape) — the early-September dollar weakness (Waller, a ~3% yen surge) has reversed.
active_narratives.thesis: The ECB is in a tightening bias, not an easing one: 25bp on Jun 11 to a 2.25% deposit rate, held on Jul 23 with some governors questioning whether more was warranted (a 'unanimous' vote characterization is unverified — drop it). July was a non-projection meeting so the bar to move was structurally higher; Sep 10 carries fresh forecasts and is the live decision, with the July FINAL HICP confirmed at 2.9% (Aug 20 fetch) and the August flash ~Aug 31 as the last major input. Energy-driven inflation is the shared driver with the Fed, so the policy-RATE gap is narrowing even as near-term direction diverges — the euro-weakness-on-divergence leg is the part of this narrative most at risk of being wrong, and it is now measurably inverted. Eurozone data keeps supporting the hike case: Q2 GDP +0.4% QoQ / +1.0% YoY CONFIRMED UNREVISED at the Aug 14 second estimate (employment +0.1% QoQ), and the August HICP jumped to 3.2% headline (FINAL, Eurostat Sep 17 — the 3.3% flash was revised down) entirely on energy (+14.3%) while core EASED to 2.4% and services to 3.0% (from 3.3%) — services is the component the ECB actually watches, and it is now moving the DOVISH way, which is why a Reuters poll (Sep 3) has economists at one-and-done after Sep 10 while markets price another move by December; Nagel (Sep 1-2) called September 'clearly warranted' but was cautious beyond it; Lagarde (Dublin, Sep 18, RTÉ interview): rates are decided meeting by meeting, 'cutting rates is very unlikely at the moment', growth 'a little more promising' than expected, no second-round effects seen yet — a tightening bias into Oct 28-29 with no pre-commitment. The Sep 10 staff projections revised 2027-28 inflation UP and 2026-27 growth UP versus June. Global duration headwinds across developed markets still hold as a conclusion, but because everyone is tightening, not because the Fed is an outlier.

active_narratives.title: US-Iran Hormuz Blockade Escalation: Oil Supply Crisis Resurfaces
active_narratives.summary: US naval blockade of Iranian ports and the Hormuz disruption are INTACT as of Sep 18, 2026, and the conflict re-escalated into the biggest exchange of fire since July: US strikes on IRGC launchers on Larak Island (Aug 30) and on southern-coast air-defence, radar and mine-laying assets (Sep 1); Iranian missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq, and from Sep 3 the UAE (no US casualties; Iran reports 12-18 dead including a wedding party in Sirik, under CENTCOM investigation); two Saudi-crude tankers struck in the strait (Aug 30/Sep 1). Sep 5: IRGC ballistic missiles fired at two US Navy warships — the first such attack, no hits (CENTCOM) — answered by the disabling of the Iranian tankers Downy and Stark 1 and the destruction of the Kylo (Sep 5-6) and the sinking of the Aframax Riesco (Sep 9); Iran's SNSC said it would declare a restricted maritime zone from the blockade line through Hormuz. Sep 14-15: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was suspended after a reported attack, pushing Red Sea-routed barrels back through Hormuz, and Libya's NOC shut two fields on protests — Brent hit a four-month high near 106 on Sep 15, then fell three straight sessions as Aramco signalled roughly half of pipeline flows restored. CENTCOM tally: 103 vessels redirected since Jul 14 (Sep 15; 94 on Sep 7-8, 87 on Sep 3). NAME THE METRIC: Kpler's visible commodity-vessel count was 5-11/day in early September (10-day average 13 vs ~100 ships and ~20 mb/d pre-war — Al Jazeera/Kpler Sep 3; independent trackers put mid-September crossings near 11-12/day) — but oil VOLUME is near pre-war (more than 17M bbl on Aug 31 vs a 21.6 mb/d pre-war average; ~15M bbl on Sep 2 per Vance) because CENTCOM declared the strait mine-free on Aug 27 and traffic uses the southern route. There is NO ceasefire and never was one in August (the Jun 17 memorandum's 60-day window expired Aug 17 with no deal); Bloomberg (Sep 4): 'We Are Stalled' — both sides far from formal talks and raising preconditions. The Oman corridor track is ALIVE, not dead: after the early-September fee dispute, Iran and Oman agreed a temporary-lane plan in principle, announced by Araghchi in Beijing alongside Wang Yi on Sep 16 as China pressed publicly for reopening — but Araghchi (Sep 13) said the Oman deal alone does NOT reopen the strait (Iran's condition is a US return to the Islamabad MoU), and the plan is reported stalled on Saudi objections (Sep 18). Sanctions lane: Treasury's 'Operation Economic Outcast' launched Aug 24 (60+ entities, individuals and vessels across Iran, Turkiye, Hong Kong, India, UAE and Singapore; five new sectoral sanctions — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, shipping; Bank Melli branches to close globally), with follow-on tranches Aug 28 (a UAE individual plus a Hong Kong trader) Sep 4 (three Golden Global entities, Istanbul), Sep 8, Sep 10 (19 targets across Iraq, Lebanon and the UAE plus a presumption-of-denial licensing policy for Iran-related applications), Sep 14 and Sep 17 (a digital-asset exchange incl. BITBANK, secondary-sanctions designation) — cadence now faster than weekly; the UAE's Aug 19 financial embargo on Iran stands. WTI 101.16 (Sep 17, pipeline tape; +19% m/m) / Brent 103.87 (Sep 18), off the Sep 15 Brent high near 106; April peak close 112.95 (Apr 7; intraday 117.63).
active_narratives.thesis: The load-bearing tension has moved again: the premium is re-arming on PHYSICAL change, not headlines alone — mines cleared but tankers hit, coastal radar degraded, LNG cargoes shifted to ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, Saudi exports diving (Sep 2). Do not read falling crude as the strait reopening (Sep 3 is the model case: WTI printed 89.57 on Trump's 'won't last long' remark and still CLOSED UP at 91.30), and do not read 'ceasefire expires' or 'peace deal' headlines as state changes — no operative ceasefire or deal exists. Two metrics disagree and reports must name which: vessel COUNT is ~-90% vs pre-war while barrel VOLUME is ~70-80% of pre-war. Offsets: Venezuela — Chevron ($7B pledge), ENI and GE signed deals under US oversight on Sep 2 (CONFIRMED) while the US claim on reserves remains a presidential announcement (REPORTED); OFAC amended the Venezuela general licences Sep 14 and Sep 16, so that leg is moving — the only meaningful bearish supply leg in the window. Sell-side bands sit BELOW spot and are dated: Goldman's $85 Brent / $79 WTI 2026 average is a MARCH revision (its Apr 26 note lifted Q4 Brent to $90 / WTI $83 and 2027 to $85/$80), Citi Q3 Brent $86 (Sep 3), Morgan Stanley Brent $90 Q3 to ~$100 Q4, JPMorgan $86/$80 on a reopening base case that has not arrived — do not quote $85 as a current band against ~$104 spot. Transmission legs that still apply: logistics-cost inflation from rerouting pressures semiconductor supply chains (ASML, TSM, MU); record US diesel prices (Sep 3) fed the inflation impulse behind the Fed's Sep 16 hike (the rate path lives in fed_rate_pivot — do not carry a separate figure here). Falsifiable both ways: further strikes or a new sanctions tranche (cadence now faster than weekly) re-arm the premium; an ACTUAL reopening to normal transit — not a permissioned corridor — would be the first genuine supply improvement and has NOT happened.

active_narratives.summary: Microsoft's disclosed 45% OpenAI share of Azure backlog is a DECEMBER-quarter figure that has never been refreshed — do not quote it as current; the closest refresh is Hood's Q4 remark that commercial RPO grew +25% EXCLUDING OpenAI, with all sequential RPO growth from customers outside the frontier-model companies. The exclusivity unwind was TWO stages, not one late-April event: Microsoft's compute right-of-first-refusal ended Oct 28, 2025 (Microsoft blog, primary), and the residual Azure API exclusivity ended ~Apr 27, 2026 (REPORTED — trade-press convergence; GPT-5.5 appeared on Amazon Bedrock Apr 28), so OpenAI can now buy compute elsewhere. Q4 FY2026 printed Jul 29, 2026: commercial RPO $678B (+84% YoY) and Azure +43% constant currency, both ahead of the prior $627B/~40%. AZURE IS NO LONGER AN UNDISCLOSED LINE: the reporting overhaul LANDED on Sep 2, 2026 (8-K Items 7.01/9.01, Ex. 99.1, primary) — Azure FY26 $101.938B (+40%) vs FY25 $72.610B, Q4 FY26 $29.417B (+42%), Q1 FY27 guided 44-45% constant currency, capex 'over $50 billion'. The recast Q4 number is +42%, not the +43% above, because GitHub cloud, developer services and Security Copilot moved to M365 Commercial Cloud — so 'Azure growth ex-OpenAI' is now trackable rather than anticipated.
active_narratives.thesis: Single-vendor concentration risk is real but has moved on two axes since this was written. With exclusivity fully unwound (ROFR Oct 2025, API exclusivity Apr 2026), the forward question is no longer lock-in but whether OpenAI-linked Azure consumption DECELERATES now that it can buy elsewhere — the cleaner read on calls is Azure growth ex-OpenAI, and the RPO-ex-OpenAI +25% disclosure is the first partial refresh of the concentration picture. Microsoft is also actively reducing the dependency with in-house MAI models — but the '89% cheaper than OpenAI' figure is Microsoft's own self-reported GPU-cost reduction for MAI-Voice-2-Flash in Dynamics 365 Contact Center ONLY, not API pricing and not portfolio-wide; do not generalize it. Capex is the swing factor: $175B for CALENDAR 2026 restated (from ~$190B — a useful-life reclass, spend unchanged, NOT a cut, and NOT an FY2027 figure), with memory prices as the cost driver — a direct link to the memory-supercycle narrative, now confirmed from outside Microsoft by Amazon naming higher memory costs as the reason for its ~$200B to ~$220B raise on Jul 30. active_narratives.title: BigTech AI Strategy Divergence: GOOG TPU Upgrade vs MSFT/AMZN Caution
active_narratives.summary: Market differentiating BigTech AI exposure by structure rather than by any single day's rating: GOOG's in-house TPU stack, MSFT's OpenAI/Azure concentration, AMZN's capex load. Signal states across the three have churned repeatedly -- GOOG ran BUY to CAUTION to HOLD between June and late July -- so the durable content here is the structural split, not a signal triple that decays within days.
active_narratives.thesis: Divergence reflects structural AI strategy differences. GOOG benefits from owning its accelerator roadmap -- Ironwood GA, with 8th-gen Sunfish/Zebrafish only in select-customer preview and GA not until late 2027 -- and raised FY26 capex to $195-205B (NOT the '>=$180B' an earlier update recorded: $180-190B was the PRIOR guide). MSFT's OpenAI concentration is the most-cited risk but has softened -- the late-April rewrite ended cloud exclusivity and MSFT is shipping in-house models it says cut costs up to 89% -- and the 45% Azure-backlog share is a December-quarter figure never refreshed, so it should not be quoted as current. AMZN carries ~$220B FY26 capex (raised from ~$200B on 30 July, attributed to higher memory costs) against a genuine AWS reacceleration -- Q2 AWS grew 37% to $42.2B, its fastest since Q4 2021. The Jul 22-30 print window has now CLOSED and all three reported, so the June framing is superseded: the actuals show all three still raising or holding capex with none guiding down, and the divergence now runs on who funds it from operating cash and who is paying input-cost inflation for the same capacity.

active_narratives.title: FTC and States Sue Amazon Over Ad-Price Manipulation
active_narratives.summary: FTC and 22 states sued Amazon on Mon Aug 31, 2026 in W.D. Washington (2:26-cv-03097) — a Section 5 FTC Act DECEPTION/unfairness case plus state UDAP claims, NOT antitrust: Amazon told advertisers they would pay one cent above the second-highest bid but from 2019 ran an undisclosed 'soft reserve'/phantom-bidder floor, charging winners their full bid on ~80% of auctions by 2024 (Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Display); the FTC release says 'tens of billions of dollars' and the complaint says 'billions' — neither primary contains the '>$20B' figure previously carried here — across approximately 1.2 million advertising customers (complaint para 1). Amazon called the suit 'misguided' the same day; AMZN fell ~3% (reported). Amazon's pipeline signal flipped CAUTION→HOLD the same day, but that flip was the >5%-extension entry block CLEARING at +3.1% vs the 50-day — mechanical, unrelated to the suit.
active_narratives.thesis: Regulatory overhang on Amazon's highest-margin line: a deception case on auction mechanics can force disclosure/pricing changes and refunds rather than structural remedies, so the near-term read is ad-revenue yield risk and headline risk, not a break-up threat. No procedural dates published yet (standard 21-day answer clock from service). The same-day HOLD signal was an entry-block clearance, not a pipeline verdict on the lawsuit — do not read it as 'impact priced'.
